```{r, include = FALSE}
# The chunks run against the Spark Connect server in SPARK_REMOTE: the
# site's build starts Spark 4.2.1 in a container and sets it. The DuckDB
# section also needs duckdb and arrow.
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
  eval = nzchar(Sys.getenv("SPARK_REMOTE"))
)
```

SparkR and sparklyr reach Spark through a local Spark installation and its
JVM; pysparklyr reaches Spark Connect through Python. zuspark needs none
of them. Spark Connect is gRPC carrying protocol buffers, with results as
Arrow record batches, and each of those has an R implementation:

* **gRPC** through [zugrpc](https://github.com/pedrobtz/zugrpc), on
  [zuhttp](https://github.com/pedrobtz/zuhttp)'s HTTP/2 and the operating
  system's TLS.
* **Protocol buffers** through
  [zuproto](https://github.com/pedrobtz/zuproto), which reads Spark's
  message definitions at run time from a compiled descriptor set that
  zuspark ships, pinned to one Spark release.
* **Arrow** through [zuarrow](https://github.com/pedrobtz/zuarrow), which
  decodes the batches and converts them to R, refusing a value R cannot
  hold exactly unless you say otherwise.

zuspark itself is R code over these packages: it has no compiled code of
its own. `zuspark_info()` shows what it was built with.

```{r setup}
library(zuspark)
zuspark_info()
```

## What a query costs

A query is two round trips. `spark_sql()` sends the statement and gets
back the server's plan for it, unexecuted; `spark_collect()` or
`spark_fetch()` executes that plan and reads the result as it streams.
The server keeps the result buffered until the client says it is done
with it, so that a stream cut by a proxy or a timeout can be reattached
where it stopped. zuspark releases what it has read as it goes, and the
rest when the query finishes or fails.

```{r}
con <- spark_connect()
q <- spark_sql(con, "SELECT id, id % 7 AS weekday, rand(42) AS amount FROM range(1000000)")
system.time(df <- spark_collect(q))
nrow(df)
q
```

## A Spark result in DuckDB

`spark_fetch()` returns the result as an Arrow stream rather than a data
frame. Code that consumes Arrow can take it from there without the rows
becoming R vectors first. DuckDB is one such consumer: here a summary is
computed by Spark, and joined in DuckDB with a table that only exists
locally.

DuckDB's R package registers Arrow data through the arrow package, so
the stream is converted to an arrow `RecordBatchReader` first. Loading
nanoarrow provides that conversion.

```{r}
library(DBI)
invisible(loadNamespace("nanoarrow"))

totals <- spark_sql(con, "
  SELECT id % 7 AS weekday, count(*) AS orders, sum(id % 100) / 100 AS total
  FROM range(1000000)
  GROUP BY id % 7
")

local <- dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb(shared_home = FALSE))
duckdb::duckdb_register_arrow(
  local, "spark_totals",
  arrow::as_record_batch_reader(spark_fetch(totals))
)

dbWriteTable(local, "days", data.frame(
  weekday = 0:6,
  name = c("Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri", "Sat", "Sun")
))

dbGetQuery(local, "
  SELECT d.name, t.orders, t.total
  FROM spark_totals t JOIN days d USING (weekday)
  ORDER BY weekday
")
dbDisconnect(local, shutdown = TRUE)
```

The batches arrive in R as Arrow bytes, and DuckDB reads them from there;
they are never converted to R vectors. They are on the R heap as bytes
for as long as the stream lives, though: decoding each batch as it
arrives is planned for a later version.

```{r}
spark_disconnect(con)
```
